case: A 63-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of difficulty swallowing. It began with solid foods and now occurs with soft foods. He has had a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss during this period. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 45 years and drinks 6 to 8 beers daily. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg. He appears thin. Upper endoscopy shows an ulcerated, friable mass that narrows the lumen of the middle third of the esophagus, 28 cm from the incisors. Biopsy specimens show invasive nests of atypical squamous cells with keratin pearls. Diagnosis: squamous cell carcinoma of the middle third of the esophagus.

questions.stem: Three months later, he has paroxysms of coughing each time he drinks liquids, and he develops right lower lobe pneumonia. His voice is unchanged. Which of the following most likely explains these new findings?
options: Aspiration of gastric acid refluxing above a distal stricture
Erosion of the tumor into the adjacent airway
Paralysis of a vocal fold from recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion
Hematogenous spread of tumor to the right lower lobe
approach: Place the tumor: the middle third of the esophagus lies directly behind the trachea and the left main bronchus.
Note the key clue: coughing that starts with every swallow of liquid points to a direct channel between the esophagus and the airway.
Use the normal voice to rule out recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, then pick erosion into the airway (an acquired tracheoesophageal or bronchoesophageal fistula).
questions.why: Squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus favors the upper and middle thirds, where the esophagus touches the trachea and left main bronchus. The esophagus has no serosa, so the tumor invades neighboring structures early. When it erodes into the airway, swallowed liquid passes straight into the bronchi, which causes coughing with each swallow and aspiration pneumonia. Smoking and heavy alcohol use are the main risk factors for this tumor type, while adenocarcinoma arises in the distal third from Barrett esophagus.
whyNot: Reflux above a stricture can cause aspiration, but it tends to happen when lying down or at night. It does not start the moment liquid is swallowed, and his tumor is in the middle third, not at the gastroesophageal junction.
Correct.
Invasion of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve can cause aspiration, but it also causes hoarseness. His voice is normal.
Blood-borne metastasis to the lung forms nodules. It does not explain coughing that is triggered by drinking.

topics: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma versus adenocarcinoma

questions.stem: He undergoes esophagectomy with removal of the distal esophagus through the diaphragm. After surgery, he has delayed gastric emptying. Division of which of the following structures, with its diaphragmatic opening and vertebral level, best explains this complication?
options: Thoracic duct, through the aortic hiatus at T12
Right phrenic nerve, through the caval opening at T8
Azygos vein, through the aortic hiatus at T12
Vagal trunks, through the esophageal hiatus at T10
approach: Link delayed gastric emptying to loss of parasympathetic supply to the stomach.
Recall which structures pass through the diaphragm with the esophagus: the anterior and posterior vagal trunks at T10.
Check the other openings: inferior vena cava at T8; aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein at T12.
questions.why: The anterior and posterior vagal trunks run on the esophagus and pass with it through the esophageal hiatus at about T10. They carry parasympathetic fibers that drive gastric motility and relaxation of the pylorus. Removing the distal esophagus divides both trunks, so the stomach empties slowly. A common memory aid is 'I ate ten eggs at twelve': IVC at T8, esophagus at T10, aorta at T12.
whyNot: The thoracic duct passes through the aortic hiatus at T12. Injury causes chylothorax, a milky pleural effusion, not delayed gastric emptying.
The right phrenic nerve is associated with the caval opening at T8. It supplies the diaphragm, and injury paralyzes the right hemidiaphragm.
The azygos vein passes through the aortic hiatus at T12. It drains the posterior chest wall and has no role in gastric motility.
Correct.

questions.stem: His tumor arose from esophageal surface epithelium. The trachea and esophagus both develop from the foregut in the fourth week. Which of the following components of the trachea arises from the same germ layer as the epithelium in which his tumor began?
options: Seromucous glands of the submucosa
C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage
Smooth muscle of the trachealis
Fibroelastic connective tissue of the wall
approach: Identify the germ layer of esophageal epithelium: foregut endoderm.
Recall that the lung bud grows from the ventral foregut, so the airway lining and its glands are also endoderm.
Separate these from the wall tissues (cartilage, smooth muscle, connective tissue), which come from splanchnic mesoderm.
questions.why: The respiratory diverticulum buds from the ventral wall of the foregut in week 4. Its endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the larynx, trachea, bronchi, and alveoli, and the glands that grow down from that lining. The surrounding splanchnic mesoderm forms the cartilage, smooth muscle, and connective tissue. The esophageal epithelium comes from the same foregut endoderm.
whyNot: Correct.
Tracheal cartilage forms from splanchnic mesoderm around the lung bud, not from endoderm.
The trachealis muscle forms from splanchnic mesoderm. The same is true of bronchial smooth muscle.
The connective tissue of the airway wall comes from splanchnic mesoderm.

questions.stem: Sequencing of his tumor shows an inactivating TP53 mutation with a G to T transversion, a change linked to benzo[a]pyrene in tobacco smoke. Loss of the normal product of this gene most directly allows which of the following in cells with DNA damage?
options: Constitutive activation of RAS GTPase signaling
Accumulation of replication errors in microsatellites
Entry into S phase before the damage is repaired
Stabilization of beta-catenin in the cytoplasm
approach: Recall the job of p53: it senses DNA damage and halts the cell cycle at the G1 to S checkpoint.
Trace the pathway: p53 induces p21, which inhibits cyclin-CDK complexes, which keeps Rb active and holds E2F in check.
Predict the result of losing p53: damaged cells keep dividing and pass mutations on.
questions.why: Normal p53 is stabilized when DNA is damaged. It turns on p21, a CDK inhibitor, so Rb stays underphosphorylated and keeps E2F bound, which blocks the G1 to S transition. This pause allows repair, and if the damage is too great, p53 triggers apoptosis. Without p53, cells with damaged DNA enter S phase and copy their mutations. Benzo[a]pyrene forms bulky adducts on guanine, and misrepair produces the G to T changes often found in TP53 of smoking-related cancers.
whyNot: Constant RAS signaling comes from a gain-of-function mutation in a RAS gene, an oncogene. Losing p53 does not activate RAS.
Microsatellite errors build up when mismatch repair genes such as MLH1 or MSH2 are lost, as in Lynch syndrome.
Correct.
Beta-catenin builds up when APC is lost, as in colorectal cancer. This is a separate pathway from p53.

topics: p53 and the G1 to S checkpoint

case: A 58-year-old woman comes to the physician because of hoarseness that has worsened steadily for 3 months. She has no pain or difficulty swallowing. She has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years and drinks 2 to 3 glasses of wine daily. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 138/84 mm Hg. No cervical lymph nodes are palpable. Flexible laryngoscopy shows an irregular, white, exophytic lesion on the anterior two thirds of the right true vocal fold. Both vocal folds move normally. Biopsy specimens show invasive nests of atypical squamous cells with keratin pearls. Diagnosis: glottic squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx.

questions.stem: Her 6-year-old grandson has a 1-year history of hoarseness. Laryngoscopy shows multiple soft, wartlike, exophytic lesions on both vocal folds, and the lesions have recurred twice after surgical removal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the grandson's lesions?
options: Repetitive phonotrauma from vocal overuse
Latent Epstein-Barr virus infection
Human papillomavirus types 6 and 11
Human papillomavirus types 16 and 18
approach: Note the features: a child, multiple wartlike lesions, and repeated recurrence after removal.
Name the lesion: juvenile (recurrent respiratory) laryngeal papillomatosis.
Match it to the low-risk HPV types that cause benign papillomas: types 6 and 11.
questions.why: Juvenile laryngeal papillomatosis is caused by HPV types 6 and 11, usually acquired from the mother during birth. The lesions are benign squamous papillomas, often multiple, and they recur after removal. They rarely become malignant. In contrast, his grandmother's tumor is a squamous cell carcinoma driven by smoking and alcohol, and on the glottis it causes hoarseness early, while still small.
whyNot: Voice overuse causes vocal fold nodules, which are small, smooth, and usually bilateral at the junction of the anterior and middle thirds. They are not wartlike and do not keep recurring after removal if voice use changes.
Epstein-Barr virus is linked to nasopharyngeal carcinoma and some lymphomas, not to laryngeal papillomas.
Correct.
HPV types 16 and 18 are high-risk types linked to oropharyngeal and cervical carcinoma. Benign papillomas come from the low-risk types.

topics: Laryngeal papillomatosis versus vocal fold nodules

questions.stem: Which of the following epithelia normally covers the site where her tumor arose?
options: Nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium
Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium
Simple cuboidal epithelium with microvilli
approach: Locate the tumor: the glottis, meaning the true vocal fold.
Recall that surfaces exposed to friction (vocal folds, oropharynx) are lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
Connect this squamous lining to squamous cell carcinoma as the main laryngeal cancer. Keratin pearls in a tumor show squamous differentiation, not a keratinized normal lining.
questions.why: The true vocal folds rub together thousands of times a day, so they are covered by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium, like the oropharynx. Most of the rest of the larynx, including the false vocal folds, has pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium. Squamous cell carcinoma makes up the great majority of laryngeal cancers. Well-differentiated squamous carcinomas often form keratin pearls even when the lining they came from was nonkeratinized.
whyNot: Correct.
Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium covers the skin. The keratin pearls in her tumor reflect squamous differentiation of the cancer, not the normal fold lining.
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium lines the false vocal folds, ventricles, and trachea. It is absent from the free edge of the true fold.
Simple cuboidal epithelium lines small ducts and the smallest bronchioles. It is not found on the vocal folds.

questions.stem: Cigarette smoke exposes her airway epithelium to superoxide and hydrogen peroxide. Her serum selenium concentration is low. Reduced activity of which of the following enzymes would most impair her epithelial cells' removal of hydrogen peroxide and lipid hydroperoxides?
options: Catalase
Copper-zinc superoxide dismutase
Myeloperoxidase
Glutathione peroxidase
approach: List the main antioxidant enzymes: superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione peroxidase.
Pick the one that needs selenium: glutathione peroxidase has selenocysteine in its active site.
Confirm that it handles both hydrogen peroxide and lipid hydroperoxides, using reduced glutathione.
questions.why: Smoke and high inspired oxygen both increase reactive oxygen species in the lung. Superoxide dismutase turns superoxide into hydrogen peroxide. Glutathione peroxidase then reduces hydrogen peroxide and lipid hydroperoxides to water and alcohols, using reduced glutathione. This enzyme contains selenocysteine, so selenium deficiency lowers its activity and leaves membranes open to lipid peroxidation.
whyNot: Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide, but it is a heme enzyme that needs iron, not selenium, and it does not act on lipid hydroperoxides.
Copper-zinc superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide. It needs copper and zinc.
Myeloperoxidase in neutrophils makes hypochlorous acid from hydrogen peroxide. It creates oxidants to kill microbes, so it does not protect cells.
Correct.

questions.stem: She has also had frequent episodes of acute bronchitis. Which of the following defenses that normally clear inhaled particles of 2 to 10 micrometers from the bronchi is most directly impaired by smoking?
options: Opsonization by surfactant proteins A and D
Mucociliary clearance by ciliated epithelium
Secretory IgA binding at the mucosal surface
Filtration of particles by the nasal turbinates
approach: Match particle size to deposition site: particles of 2 to 10 micrometers settle in the trachea and bronchi.
Recall the defense that removes them there: mucus traps them and cilia sweep them up to the pharynx.
Link smoking to paralysis and loss of cilia and to goblet cell hyperplasia, which slows this escalator.
questions.why: Larger particles are filtered in the nose, mid-size particles land in the bronchi, and particles under about 2 micrometers reach the alveoli. In the bronchi, the mucociliary escalator traps particles and microbes in mucus and moves them toward the pharynx. Smoke slows ciliary beating, destroys ciliated cells, and increases thick mucus. Retained mucus and microbes lead to repeated bronchitis and pneumonia.
whyNot: Surfactant proteins A and D act as opsonins in the alveoli. They handle the smallest particles that reach the gas-exchange surface, not those in the bronchi.
Correct.
Secretory IgA blocks microbes from attaching to the mucosa. It does not physically remove deposited particles, and smoking does not mainly act through it.
The nasal turbinates filter particles larger than about 10 micrometers before they reach the lower airways.

dx: Malignant pleural mesothelioma with asbestos pleural plaques
case: A 71-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of dull right-sided chest pain, increasing shortness of breath, and a 7-kg (15-lb) weight loss. He worked as a pipefitter in a shipyard from 1972 to 1985. He has never smoked. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Examination shows dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds over the lower right chest. CT of the chest shows a thick, nodular rind of pleural tissue encasing the right lung, a moderate right pleural effusion, and calcified plaques on the parietal pleura of both hemidiaphragms. Thoracentesis yields bloody exudative fluid. Pleural biopsy specimens show an infiltrating epithelioid malignancy. Diagnosis: malignant pleural mesothelioma with asbestos-related pleural plaques.

questions.stem: The pathologist must distinguish his tumor from metastatic adenocarcinoma involving the pleura. Which of the following findings in the tumor cells would best support mesothelioma?
options: Positive staining for CEA and TTF-1
Intracellular mucin droplets on mucicarmine stain
Short, sparse microvilli on electron microscopy
Positive staining for calretinin and WT1
approach: Recall that both tumors can look glandular or epithelioid on routine stains.
List the markers of mesothelial cells: calretinin, WT1, and cytokeratin 5/6, with long, slender microvilli on electron microscopy.
List the markers of lung adenocarcinoma: CEA, TTF-1, mucin, and short microvilli. Pick the mesothelial pattern.
questions.why: Malignant mesothelioma arises from the mesothelial cells lining the pleura. It keeps their markers: calretinin, WT1, and cytokeratins, and on electron microscopy it shows long, slender, abundant microvilli. Adenocarcinoma spreading to the pleura makes mucin, stains for CEA and, if from the lung, TTF-1, and has short, stubby microvilli. Mesothelioma follows asbestos exposure by decades and causes a recurrent bloody effusion and a rind of tumor around the lung.
whyNot: CEA and TTF-1 positivity points to lung adenocarcinoma. Mesotheliomas are usually negative for both.
Mucin production is a feature of adenocarcinoma. Mesothelial cells do not make epithelial mucin.
Short, sparse microvilli are typical of adenocarcinoma. Mesothelioma cells have long, slender, numerous microvilli.
Correct.

questions.stem: His twin brother worked beside him in the shipyard for the same years and has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 45 years. For which of the following malignancies does the combination of these two exposures most greatly increase the brother's risk?
options: Malignant pleural mesothelioma
Bronchogenic carcinoma
Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder
Bronchial carcinoid tumor
approach: Recall which cancers asbestos causes: bronchogenic carcinoma and mesothelioma.
Recall which of these smoking also causes: bronchogenic carcinoma only.
Apply the principle: when both act on the same cancer, the risks multiply, so lung carcinoma risk rises far more than either exposure alone would cause.
questions.why: Asbestos fibers injure the lung and pleura and increase the risk of both bronchogenic carcinoma and mesothelioma. Smoking adds to lung carcinoma risk in a synergistic way: the combined risk is much greater than the sum of the two separate risks. Smoking does not raise mesothelioma risk. Bronchogenic carcinoma is also far more common than mesothelioma among asbestos-exposed workers.
whyNot: Mesothelioma risk comes from asbestos alone. Smoking does not add to it, so the brother's mesothelioma risk is about the same as the patient's.
Correct.
Smoking raises bladder cancer risk, but asbestos does not, so there is no combined effect.
Bronchial carcinoids are neuroendocrine tumors with no strong link to smoking or asbestos.

questions.stem: Over the next month, the tumor spreads across the central part of the right hemidiaphragm, and he develops pain at the tip of the right shoulder. Which of the following nerves carries the pain sensation that is referred to his shoulder?
options: Lower intercostal nerves
Vagus nerve
Phrenic nerve
Thoracic splanchnic nerves
approach: Identify the irritated layer: parietal pleura on the central diaphragm.
Recall its sensory nerve: the phrenic nerve, from spinal segments C3 to C5.
Explain the referral: the same segments supply the skin over the shoulder through the supraclavicular nerves.
questions.why: Parietal pleura is sensitive to pain. Its costal part and the peripheral diaphragm are supplied by intercostal nerves, so pain there is felt sharply in the chest wall or upper abdomen. The central diaphragmatic and mediastinal parietal pleura are supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5). The brain reads pain from these segments as coming from the shoulder, which shares the C3 and C4 dermatomes. Visceral pleura has only autonomic supply and is insensitive to pain.
whyNot: The lower intercostal nerves supply the costal pleura and the peripheral rim of the diaphragm. Pain there is felt in the lower chest wall or abdomen, not the shoulder.
The vagus nerve carries autonomic afferents from the viscera, including visceral pleura and lungs. It does not mediate sharp pleuritic pain referred to the shoulder.
Correct.
The thoracic splanchnic nerves carry sympathetic fibers to abdominal organs. They do not supply the diaphragmatic pleura.

questions.stem: Spirometry and lung volumes are measured before treatment. Which of the following patterns is most likely? (Normal FEV1/FVC ratio is 0.70 or greater.)
options: Reduced TLC with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.85
Reduced TLC with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.55
Increased TLC with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.55
Normal TLC with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.55
approach: Identify the mechanical problem: a stiff rind of tumor and fluid prevents the lung from expanding.
Classify it as restrictive disease from outside the lung: the lung cannot fill, so TLC and FVC fall.
Predict the ratio: the airways are open, so FEV1 falls in proportion to FVC and the ratio stays normal or rises.
questions.why: A pleural rind and effusion restrict lung expansion, which is a restrictive defect. TLC, vital capacity, and FVC all fall. Because the airways are not narrowed, air still leaves quickly, so FEV1 falls about as much as FVC, and the FEV1/FVC ratio is normal or high. Obstructive disease shows the reverse: a low ratio with normal or increased TLC.
whyNot: Correct.
A low TLC with a low ratio is a mixed pattern. It would need both restriction and airway obstruction, and he has no airway disease.
An increased TLC with a low ratio is the obstructive pattern of emphysema, with air trapping and hyperinflation.
A normal TLC with a low ratio is obstruction without hyperinflation, as in asthma or chronic bronchitis.

case: A 46-year-old man who immigrated from Guangdong province in southern China comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of a painless lump in the left side of his neck. He also has a feeling of fullness and decreased hearing in the left ear and intermittent blood-tinged nasal discharge. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 124/80 mm Hg. Examination shows a firm, nontender, 3-cm left upper cervical lymph node. The left tympanic membrane is retracted with an amber middle ear effusion. Nasopharyngoscopy shows a mass in the left lateral nasopharyngeal recess. Biopsy specimens show sheets of undifferentiated, nonkeratinizing carcinoma cells mixed with many lymphocytes. Diagnosis: nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

questions.stem: In situ hybridization is performed on the tumor cells. Which of the following is most likely to be detected?
options: Epstein-Barr virus-encoded small RNAs
Human papillomavirus type 16 E6 and E7 mRNA
Human herpesvirus 8 latency-associated transcripts
Human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 proviral DNA
approach: Combine the clues: a southern Chinese patient, a nasopharyngeal mass, and undifferentiated carcinoma rich in lymphocytes.
Match this to the virus that latently infects nasopharyngeal carcinoma cells: Epstein-Barr virus.
Recall the standard tissue test: in situ hybridization for EBV-encoded small RNAs (EBER).
questions.why: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma, especially the nonkeratinizing and undifferentiated types, is almost always infected with Epstein-Barr virus. It is common in southern China and parts of Africa, where genetic, dietary, and viral factors combine. Latent EBV in tumor cells makes large amounts of small RNAs called EBERs, which in situ hybridization detects. The tumor spreads early to cervical lymph nodes, and blockage of the eustachian tube causes a one-sided serous middle ear effusion, as in this patient.
whyNot: Correct.
HPV type 16 drives squamous carcinoma of the tonsil and base of tongue in the oropharynx, not the classic undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma seen in southern Chinese patients.
Human herpesvirus 8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, primary effusion lymphoma, and multicentric Castleman disease.
HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukemia and lymphoma and a myelopathy. It is not linked to nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

questions.stem: His 38-year-old sister has had recurrent nosebleeds since childhood. She has small red macules on her lips, tongue, and fingertips that blanch with pressure, and last year she had a brain abscess. Her son has the same skin lesions. Which of the following best explains the sister's condition?
options: Autosomal dominant deficiency of von Willebrand factor
X-linked recessive deficiency of coagulation factor IX
Autosomal dominant loss of endoglin function
Autosomal dominant mutation in the fibrillin-1 gene
approach: Group the findings: recurrent epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasias, and a brain abscess, passed from mother to son.
Explain the abscess: a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation shunts venous blood around the lung filter, so bacteria reach the brain.
Name the disorder and its genetics: hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, autosomal dominant, with mutations in endoglin or ACVRL1 in TGF-beta signaling.
questions.why: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia is an autosomal dominant disorder, most often from loss of endoglin (ENG) or ACVRL1 (ALK1), both parts of TGF-beta family signaling in endothelial cells. Fragile, dilated vessels form telangiectasias in the nose, lips, and gut, and larger arteriovenous malformations form in the lungs, liver, and brain. A pulmonary AVM is a right-to-left shunt: it causes hypoxemia, and it lets clots or bacteria bypass the lung capillaries, leading to paradoxical stroke or brain abscess.
whyNot: Von Willebrand disease causes nosebleeds and mucosal bleeding from impaired platelet adhesion, but it does not cause telangiectasias or a brain abscess.
Hemophilia B is X-linked and mainly affects males, with joint and deep muscle bleeding. It does not cause telangiectasias.
Correct.
Fibrillin-1 mutations cause Marfan syndrome, with lens dislocation and aortic root dilation, not telangiectasias or AVMs.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man who has never smoked has an enlarged right tonsil and a cystic right upper cervical lymph node. Biopsy shows nonkeratinizing squamous cell carcinoma with strong, diffuse nuclear and cytoplasmic staining for p16. Which of the following viral actions most directly explains the p16 staining?
options: LMP-1 signaling that mimics an active CD40 receptor
E7 binding and inactivation of Rb protein
Tax transactivation of host growth factor genes
HBx activation of host growth-promoting genes
approach: Identify the tumor: tonsillar squamous cell carcinoma in a nonsmoker, which points to HPV type 16.
Recall the HPV oncoproteins: E6 degrades p53 and E7 binds Rb.
Link E7 to p16: with Rb inactivated, the cell loses the feedback that keeps p16 low, so p16 builds up and serves as a marker of HPV-driven tumors.
questions.why: High-risk HPV, mainly type 16, causes squamous cell carcinoma of the tonsil and base of tongue, often in younger patients who do not smoke. Viral E7 binds Rb and releases E2F, so the cell enters S phase. Normally Rb activity keeps p16 expression low, so loss of Rb leads to strong p16 overexpression, which pathologists use as a surrogate marker for HPV. Tobacco and alcohol related carcinomas of the oral cavity and pharynx usually lack p16 overexpression and often carry TP53 mutations instead.
whyNot: LMP-1 is an Epstein-Barr virus protein that mimics CD40 signaling. It drives nasopharyngeal carcinoma, as in the man described in the case, and some B-cell lymphomas.
Correct.
Tax is the transforming protein of HTLV-1 in adult T-cell leukemia and lymphoma.
HBx is a hepatitis B virus protein that contributes to hepatocellular carcinoma.

questions.stem: Several months before his diagnosis, he had a nosebleed that began after forceful nose blowing in dry winter air and stopped after 10 minutes of pinching the soft part of his nose. A branch of which of the following arteries most likely contributed to this bleeding?
options: Infraorbital branch of the maxillary artery
Ascending pharyngeal artery
Posterior lateral nasal branch of the sphenopalatine artery
Superior labial branch of the facial artery
approach: Classify the bleed: started with dry air and minor trauma, stopped with pressure on the front of the nose, so it is anterior.
Locate the anterior site: Kiesselbach area on the anterior nasal septum.
List the arteries that meet there: septal branches of the sphenopalatine, anterior ethmoidal, greater palatine, and superior labial arteries.
questions.why: About 90% of nosebleeds come from Kiesselbach area on the anterior septum. Four arteries anastomose there: the septal branch of the sphenopalatine artery, the anterior ethmoidal artery, the greater palatine artery, and the septal branch of the superior labial artery from the facial artery. The mucosa is thin and dries easily, so minor trauma makes it bleed, and pinching the soft nose compresses the site. Posterior bleeds come from sphenopalatine branches far back in the nasal cavity, are heavier, and are not controlled by anterior pressure.
whyNot: The infraorbital artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, supplies the lower eyelid, cheek, and side of the nose. It does not reach the nasal septum or Kiesselbach area.
The ascending pharyngeal artery supplies the pharynx and does not supply the anterior nasal septum.
Posterior lateral nasal branches of the sphenopalatine artery supply the back of the lateral nasal wall and are the source of posterior epistaxis, which pinching the nose does not stop.
Correct.

dx: Small cell lung carcinoma with SIADH and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome
case: A 64-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of difficulty rising from a chair and climbing stairs, dry mouth, and fatigue. Her strength improves briefly after repeated effort. She has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 50 years. Temperature is 36.7 °C (98.1 °F), pulse is 82/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg. She appears euvolemic. Hip flexors are weak. Deep tendon reflexes are decreased and increase after 10 seconds of maximal muscle contraction. Serum studies show sodium 121 mEq/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.0 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0), and osmolality 252 mOsm/kg H2O (275 to 295). Urine osmolality is 460 mOsm/kg H2O. TSH and morning cortisol concentrations are within the reference ranges. CT shows a central hilar mass with bulky mediastinal lymph nodes. Diagnosis: small cell lung carcinoma with SIADH and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.

questions.stem: Bronchoscopic biopsy specimens show sheets of small cells with scant cytoplasm, finely granular chromatin, and nuclear molding. Immunohistochemical staining of these cells is most likely to be positive for which of the following?
options: Leukocyte common antigen (CD45) and CD20
Chromogranin A and synaptophysin
Calretinin and Wilms tumor 1 protein
p40 and high-molecular-weight cytokeratin
approach: Recognize small cell carcinoma from the histology: small cells, scant cytoplasm, salt-and-pepper chromatin, and nuclear molding.
Recall its origin: neuroendocrine (Kulchitsky-type) cells with dense-core secretory granules.
Choose the neuroendocrine markers: chromogranin A and synaptophysin.
questions.why: Small cell carcinoma is a high-grade neuroendocrine tumor. It arises centrally in heavy smokers, grows fast, and spreads early, so it is usually treated as a systemic disease. Its cells contain neurosecretory granules, so they stain for chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and often CD56. The same neuroendocrine nature explains its paraneoplastic hormone secretion, such as ADH and ACTH.
whyNot: CD45 and CD20 mark B-cell lymphoma, another tumor of small round cells. Small cell carcinoma is epithelial and negative for CD45.
Correct.
Calretinin and WT1 mark mesothelial cells and mesothelioma.
p40 and high-molecular-weight cytokeratin mark squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms most likely explains her serum sodium concentration?
options: Ectopic vasopressin acting on renal V2 receptors
Ectopic ACTH driving cortisol excess and mineralocorticoid activity
PTHrP-induced hypercalcemia impairing urine concentration
Bilateral adrenal metastases abolishing aldosterone secretion
approach: Read the labs: low serum sodium and osmolality with inappropriately concentrated urine in a euvolemic patient with normal thyroid and adrenal function. This is SIADH.
Match SIADH to the lung cancer type that makes it: small cell carcinoma.
Trace the mechanism: ADH binds V2 receptors on collecting duct cells, aquaporin-2 channels insert in the apical membrane, and free water is retained.
questions.why: Small cell carcinoma can secrete ADH (vasopressin) without regard to plasma osmolality. ADH binds V2 receptors, raises cAMP, and inserts aquaporin-2 water channels in collecting duct cells. The kidney keeps reabsorbing water, so serum sodium is diluted while urine stays concentrated. Lung cancer paraneoplastic syndromes follow tumor type: SIADH, ACTH, and Lambert-Eaton with small cell; PTHrP hypercalcemia with squamous cell; and hypertrophic osteoarthropathy mostly with adenocarcinoma.
whyNot: Correct.
Ectopic ACTH, also from small cell carcinoma, raises cortisol and tends to cause hypokalemia and sodium retention, not hyponatremia. Her cortisol is normal.
PTHrP comes mainly from squamous cell carcinoma. Hypercalcemia causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus with dilute urine and a tendency to high sodium.
Loss of aldosterone would cause hyperkalemia and volume depletion. Her potassium and cortisol are normal and she is euvolemic.

topics: Paraneoplastic syndromes by lung cancer type

questions.stem: Her tumor cells express a neural protein that also appears on her motor nerve terminals, and her immune response against the tumor cross-reacts with the nerves. Which of the following best explains her weakness?
options: Antibodies to postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
Antibodies to the neuronal nuclear antigen Hu
Antibodies to muscle-specific tyrosine kinase
Antibodies to presynaptic P/Q-type calcium channels
approach: Use the clinical pattern: proximal weakness and low reflexes that improve after brief exercise, plus dry mouth.
Place the lesion presynaptically: repeated firing builds up calcium in the nerve terminal and releases more acetylcholine.
Name the antibody: against voltage-gated P/Q-type calcium channels shared by small cell tumor cells and nerve terminals.
questions.why: Small cell carcinoma cells express voltage-gated calcium channels. Antibodies made against the tumor also bind the P/Q-type channels on motor and autonomic nerve terminals. Less calcium enters with each action potential, so less acetylcholine is released, which causes proximal weakness, low reflexes, and dry mouth. Brief exercise lets calcium build up in the terminal, so strength and reflexes improve for a moment. Lung tumors can still escape these responses by lowering MHC class I and expressing PD-L1.
whyNot: Antibodies to acetylcholine receptors cause myasthenia gravis. Weakness worsens with repeated use, and eye muscles are usually involved first.
Anti-Hu antibodies with small cell carcinoma cause sensory neuronopathy and encephalomyelitis, not weakness that improves with effort.
Antibodies to muscle-specific kinase cause a form of myasthenia gravis with fatigable bulbar weakness.
Correct.

questions.stem: Myasthenia gravis was considered before the diagnosis was made. If she had myasthenia gravis instead, chest imaging would most likely have shown which of the following?
options: Posterior mediastinal neurogenic tumor
Middle mediastinal bronchogenic cyst
Anterior mediastinal thymoma
Middle mediastinal pericardial cyst
approach: Recall the mass linked to myasthenia gravis: thymoma, or thymic hyperplasia.
Place the thymus: anterior mediastinum, behind the sternum.
Match other masses to their compartments: neurogenic tumors posterior, cysts and lymph nodes middle.
questions.why: The thymus lies in the anterior (and superior) mediastinum. About 10 to 15% of patients with myasthenia gravis have a thymoma, and many more have thymic hyperplasia. Typical anterior masses are thymoma, teratoma, lymphoma, and retrosternal thyroid. The middle mediastinum holds the heart, hila, and lymph nodes, and the posterior mediastinum holds the sympathetic chain and nerve roots, where neurogenic tumors arise.
whyNot: Neurogenic tumors such as schwannoma and neuroblastoma arise from nerves in the posterior mediastinum. They are not linked to myasthenia gravis.
Bronchogenic cysts come from abnormal foregut budding and usually sit near the carina. They are not linked to myasthenia gravis.
Correct.
Pericardial cysts lie in the middle mediastinum, often at the right cardiophrenic angle, and are usually incidental findings.

dx: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung as a superior sulcus (Pancoast) tumor with PTHrP hypercalcemia
case: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of severe right shoulder pain that radiates down the inner arm to the fourth and fifth fingers, with weakness of the right hand. He also has constipation, frequent urination, and mild confusion. He has smoked 2 packs of cigarettes daily for 30 years. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 134/82 mm Hg. The right hand intrinsic muscles are weak. Serum studies show calcium 13.2 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5), phosphorus 2.1 mg/dL (2.5 to 4.5), and PTH 6 pg/mL (10 to 65). PTH-related protein is increased. CT shows a mass in the right lung apex invading the chest wall and first rib. Diagnosis: squamous cell carcinoma of the right superior sulcus (Pancoast tumor) with humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings on his biopsy specimen would most strongly support squamous cell carcinoma over other non-small-cell carcinomas?
options: Lepidic spread along intact alveolar walls
Small cells with scant cytoplasm and nuclear molding
Keratin pearls and intercellular bridges
Sheets of anaplastic cells lacking glandular or squamous features
approach: List the histologic signs of squamous differentiation: keratin production and cell-to-cell junctions.
Match the other choices to adenocarcinoma in situ, small cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma.
Pick keratin pearls with intercellular bridges (desmosomes).
questions.why: Squamous cell carcinoma shows keratinization, including keratin pearls, and intercellular bridges, which are desmosomes seen between cells. It is strongly linked to smoking, usually arises centrally from metaplastic bronchial epithelium, may cavitate, and is the lung tumor most often associated with PTHrP hypercalcemia. Large cell carcinoma is a poorly differentiated peripheral tumor with no glandular or squamous features and a poor prognosis. Adenocarcinoma is the most common type overall and forms glands or mucin.
whyNot: Lepidic growth along intact alveolar walls is a pattern of adenocarcinoma, as in adenocarcinoma in situ. It does not show squamous differentiation.
Small cells with nuclear molding are the hallmark of small cell carcinoma, which is not a non-small-cell carcinoma.
Correct.
Undifferentiated sheets of large cells without glands or keratin describe large cell carcinoma.

topics: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung

questions.stem: Two weeks later, he has drooping of the right upper eyelid, a small right pupil, and absent sweating on the right side of the face. Invasion of which of the following structures best explains these new findings?
options: Lower trunk of the brachial plexus
Right recurrent laryngeal nerve
Right phrenic nerve
Cervicothoracic sympathetic chain
approach: Recognize Horner syndrome: ptosis, miosis, and facial anhidrosis.
Recall the sympathetic path to the face: it rises from the upper thoracic cord through the sympathetic chain at the lung apex, including the stellate (cervicothoracic) ganglion.
Relate this to the apical tumor, which also explains his C8 to T1 pain and hand weakness through the lower trunk of the brachial plexus.
questions.why: A superior sulcus (Pancoast) tumor grows at the lung apex, where the lower trunk of the brachial plexus, the subclavian vessels, and the cervicothoracic sympathetic chain lie close together. Invasion of the sympathetic chain cuts the pathway to the face and eye, producing ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis on the same side. Invasion of the lower trunk (C8 and T1) causes the pain along the inner arm and weakness of the hand muscles he already has. Most Pancoast tumors are non-small-cell carcinomas.
whyNot: The lower trunk of the brachial plexus explains his arm pain and hand weakness, but it carries no sympathetic fibers to the face or eye.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes hoarseness from vocal fold paralysis.
Phrenic nerve injury paralyzes the hemidiaphragm, which shows as elevation on a radiograph.
Correct.

questions.stem: Benzo[a]pyrene from his cigarette smoke forms bulky adducts on guanine in his bronchial epithelial cells. Which of the following steps is required before benzo[a]pyrene can bind DNA?
options: Cytochrome P450 oxidation to a diol epoxide
UDP-glucuronosyltransferase conjugation to a glucuronide
Fenton reaction producing hydroxyl radicals from iron
Glutathione S-transferase conjugation to a thioether
approach: Recall that benzo[a]pyrene is a procarcinogen, inert until it is metabolized.
Identify the activating step: cytochrome P450 enzymes (such as CYP1A1, which smoke induces) oxidize it to a reactive diol epoxide.
Separate activation from detoxification: conjugation reactions make compounds water soluble so they can be excreted.
questions.why: Benzo[a]pyrene is a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon in tobacco smoke. Cytochrome P450 enzymes and epoxide hydrolase convert it to benzo[a]pyrene diol epoxide, an electrophile that binds guanine and forms bulky DNA adducts. If these are not repaired, they cause mutations, often G to T transversions, in genes such as TP53. Smoke induces CYP1A1, which speeds this activation.
whyNot: Correct.
Glucuronidation is a phase II detoxifying reaction that makes metabolites water soluble for excretion. It prevents DNA binding.
The Fenton reaction makes hydroxyl radicals from hydrogen peroxide and ferrous iron. It causes oxidative damage but is not how benzo[a]pyrene is activated.
Glutathione conjugation detoxifies reactive epoxides so they can be excreted. It removes the DNA-binding form.

topics: Phase I and phase II metabolism

questions.stem: He also has severe COPD. For several months his PaCO2 has been about 58 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45) with an arterial pH of 7.37 (normal 7.35 to 7.45). Which of the following best explains why his central chemoreceptors now drive relatively little extra ventilation at this PaCO2?
options: CO2 crosses the blood-brain barrier too slowly to reach them
Added CSF bicarbonate has returned CSF pH toward normal
They respond mainly to PaO2, which is only mildly reduced
Chronic hypercapnia destroys the medullary chemosensitive neurons
approach: Recall what central chemoreceptors sense: hydrogen ion in the CSF, which forms when CO2 diffuses in from the blood.
Notice that his arterial pH is near normal, so the kidneys have compensated, and over 1 to 2 days bicarbonate also rises in the CSF.
Conclude that CSF pH has returned toward normal, so the medullary stimulus fades and his breathing depends more on hypoxemia sensed by the carotid bodies.
questions.why: CO2 crosses the blood-brain barrier easily and forms carbonic acid in the CSF, and the hydrogen ion stimulates chemosensitive neurons in the medulla. With chronic CO2 retention, renal bicarbonate retention and transport of bicarbonate into the CSF buffer this acid, so CSF pH moves back toward normal within 1 to 2 days. The central drive then falls far below its acute level. The carotid and aortic bodies respond mainly to PaO2 below about 60 mm Hg, so hypoxemia becomes a larger share of his drive to breathe.
whyNot: CO2 is lipid soluble and crosses the blood-brain barrier rapidly. That is why central chemoreceptors respond to acute hypercapnia within minutes.
Correct.
Central chemoreceptors do not sense oxygen. Hypoxemia is detected by the carotid and aortic bodies.
Chronic hypercapnia does not destroy these neurons. Their response returns if CSF pH falls again.

case: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a chronic productive cough and three episodes of pneumonia in the past 2 years. He passes bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools. He had meconium ileus as a newborn. Temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 108/66 mm Hg. Height and weight are at the 5th percentile. Examination shows digital clubbing, nasal polyps, and coarse crackles over both upper lung fields. Sweat chloride concentration is 84 mmol/L on two occasions (normal less than 30; 60 or greater is diagnostic). Sputum culture grows mucoid Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Genetic testing shows homozygosity for the F508del variant of CFTR. Diagnosis: cystic fibrosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how his variant reduces CFTR function?
options: Misfolded protein held in the ER and degraded
Premature stop codon causing mRNA decay and no protein
Normal amount of surface protein with defective channel opening
Splicing defect reducing the amount of normal protein made
approach: Identify the variant: F508del, a three-base deletion that removes phenylalanine at position 508.
Recall what this does to the protein: it folds abnormally and fails ER quality control.
Predict the result: the protein is ubiquitinated and destroyed by proteasomes, so little CFTR reaches the apical membrane.
questions.why: Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disease caused by mutations in CFTR on chromosome 7. CFTR is a cAMP-regulated, ATP-gated chloride channel. The most common variant, F508del, is an in-frame deletion of three nucleotides. The protein misfolds, is held in the endoplasmic reticulum, and is degraded by the proteasome. Little chloride is secreted onto the airway surface, so the mucus becomes dehydrated and thick.
whyNot: Correct.
Premature stop codons, such as G542X, are a different class of CFTR mutation that produces no protein. F508del is an in-frame deletion, not a nonsense mutation.
Gating mutations, such as G551D, put protein on the cell surface but the channel does not open normally. F508del mainly prevents the protein from reaching the surface.
Splicing variants reduce the amount of normal protein. They are much less common than F508del and work by a different mechanism.

topics: Protein misfolding and ER quality control

questions.stem: His sweat chloride is high because chloride cannot be reabsorbed from the lumen of the sweat duct. In his airways, the same defect has a different effect on the luminal fluid. Which of the following best explains his dehydrated airway surface liquid?
options: Reduced chloride reabsorption, which leaves salt in the airway lumen
Reduced chloride secretion with increased ENaC sodium absorption
Excess sodium secretion through apical CFTR channels
Increased bicarbonate secretion that draws water from the lumen
approach: Recall the normal role of CFTR in each tissue: in the sweat duct it reabsorbs chloride, and in the airway it secretes chloride.
Predict the airway result: no chloride secretion, and loss of CFTR's restraint on ENaC lets sodium absorption increase.
Follow the water: salt leaves the lumen and water follows it, so the airway surface liquid shrinks and mucus thickens.
questions.why: CFTR moves chloride in opposite directions in different tissues. In the sweat duct, it reabsorbs chloride from the lumen, and sodium follows. Without it, salt stays in the sweat, so sweat is salty. In the airway, CFTR secretes chloride into the lumen, and it also normally restrains the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC). Without CFTR, chloride secretion stops and sodium absorption increases, so salt and water are pulled out of the airway surface liquid. Cilia cannot beat in the thin, dry layer, and mucus builds up.
whyNot: Failed reabsorption is the defect in the sweat duct. In the airway it would leave more salt and water in the lumen, which is the opposite of what happens.
Correct.
CFTR is a chloride (and bicarbonate) channel. It does not secrete sodium, and in CF the problem is too much sodium absorption.
CFTR also carries bicarbonate, and in CF bicarbonate secretion falls. Secreted bicarbonate would draw water into the lumen, not out of it.

topics: CFTR in sweat duct versus airway

questions.stem: He asks about having children in the future. Which of the following findings is he most likely to have as an adult?
options: Low testosterone with small, firm testes
Immotile sperm from absent dynein arms
Azoospermia with absent vasa deferentia
Anosmia with low gonadotropin concentrations
approach: Recall that CFTR is needed for normal development of the wolffian duct structures.
Predict the finding: congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens, so sperm cannot leave the testes.
Note that testes and testosterone are normal, so this is obstructive azoospermia.
questions.why: About 95% of men with cystic fibrosis are infertile because the vasa deferentia are absent or blocked by thick secretions in fetal life. Their testes make sperm and testosterone normally, so semen has no sperm (obstructive azoospermia). Sperm can be retrieved from the testis for assisted reproduction. Other features of CF include meconium ileus, pancreatic insufficiency with steatorrhea, chronic Pseudomonas and Staphylococcus aureus infection, bronchiectasis, and nasal polyps.
whyNot: Small, firm testes with low testosterone suggest Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), which is a testicular failure.
Immotile sperm from missing dynein arms is primary ciliary dyskinesia. It also causes chronic sinus and lung infection, but sweat chloride is normal.
Correct.
Anosmia with low gonadotropins is Kallmann syndrome, from failed migration of GnRH neurons.

questions.stem: Despite pancreatic enzyme replacement, he has trouble seeing at night, and his conjunctivae are dry with small foamy gray patches. Deficiency of this vitamin most likely contributes to his recurrent pulmonary infections through which of the following effects?
options: Impaired gamma-carboxylation of hepatic clotting factors
Oxidative damage to neuronal and erythrocyte membranes
Defective hydroxylation of proline residues in collagen
Squamous metaplasia of ciliated airway epithelium
approach: Identify the vitamin: night blindness and Bitot spots point to vitamin A deficiency.
Explain why he lacks it: pancreatic insufficiency causes fat malabsorption, so fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K are poorly absorbed.
Recall the airway effect: without retinoic acid, ciliated and mucus-secreting epithelium turns into keratinizing squamous epithelium, which weakens mucociliary clearance.
questions.why: Vitamin A, as retinoic acid, keeps specialized epithelia differentiated. In deficiency, the ciliated columnar epithelium of the airways undergoes squamous metaplasia and loses cilia and goblet cells, so mucociliary clearance fails and infections rise. In the eye, the same change causes xerophthalmia and Bitot spots, and too little rhodopsin forms in the rods, which causes night blindness. In cystic fibrosis, pancreatic insufficiency causes fat malabsorption and deficiency of all the fat-soluble vitamins.
whyNot: Gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors needs vitamin K. Deficiency causes bleeding, not night blindness or infection.
Membrane protection from oxidants needs vitamin E. Deficiency causes neuropathy, ataxia, and hemolysis.
Collagen proline hydroxylation needs vitamin C, which is water soluble and not lost through fat malabsorption.
Correct.

dx: Esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula
case: A male newborn is evaluated in the nursery 3 hours after birth at 36 weeks' gestation because of excessive drooling and an episode of coughing, choking, and cyanosis during his first feed. The pregnancy was complicated by polyhydramnios. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 156/min, respirations are 58/min, and blood pressure is 64/40 mm Hg. Frothy secretions are present at the mouth. A nasogastric tube cannot be passed beyond 10 cm from the nostril. Chest and abdominal radiographs show the tube coiled in an upper esophageal pouch and air in the stomach and bowel. Diagnosis: esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula.

questions.stem: Before surgical repair, a careful examination is done to look for associated anomalies. Which of the following is most likely to be found?
options: Macroglossia with an umbilical hernia
Bilateral cleft lip and palate
Hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle
Imperforate anus
approach: Recall that esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula is part of the VACTERL association.
List the components: vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, and limb (radial) anomalies.
Pick the option that belongs to this group: imperforate anus.
questions.why: Esophageal atresia with a distal fistula is the most common form of tracheoesophageal fistula. The fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid into the gut, so polyhydramnios develops. After birth, the baby drools and chokes with feeds, the tube stops in the blind pouch, and air reaches the stomach through the distal fistula. About half of these infants have other anomalies, often from the VACTERL group, so the anus, spine, heart, kidneys, and radial limbs are checked.
whyNot: Macroglossia with an umbilical hernia suggests Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, which is not part of VACTERL.
Cleft lip and palate come from failed fusion of facial processes. They are not part of VACTERL.
Pyloric stenosis presents at 2 to 6 weeks with projectile vomiting and is not part of VACTERL.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following embryologic errors most likely caused his anomaly?
options: Failed recanalization of the second part of the duodenum
Incomplete closure of the pleuroperitoneal canals
Faulty fusion of the tracheoesophageal ridges
Persistent communication of the vitelline duct
approach: Recall how the trachea and esophagus separate: tracheoesophageal ridges grow in and fuse to form the tracheoesophageal septum.
Predict the effect of faulty septation: the septum deviates posteriorly, the esophagus ends in a blind pouch, and the lower esophagus stays connected to the trachea.
Rule out errors in other foregut or midgut structures.
questions.why: In weeks 4 and 5, the lung bud and foregut are partly separated by tracheoesophageal ridges, which fuse to form the tracheoesophageal septum. The trachea and lung bud lie ventral and the esophagus dorsal. If the septum deviates posteriorly or forms incompletely, the upper esophagus ends blindly and the lower esophagus stays connected to the trachea. This is esophageal atresia with a distal fistula.
whyNot: Failed recanalization of the duodenum causes duodenal atresia with a double bubble sign and bilious vomiting, which is often seen with Down syndrome.
Incomplete closure of the pleuroperitoneal canals causes a posterolateral congenital diaphragmatic hernia.
Correct.
A persistent vitelline duct causes a Meckel diverticulum or an umbilical fistula, not an airway connection.

questions.stem: Chest CT before surgery shows an incidental 3-cm mass of lung tissue in the posterior basal segment of the left lower lobe. It is supplied by an artery that arises from the descending thoracic aorta and has no connection to the bronchial tree. Which of the following is this lesion most likely to cause later in childhood?
options: Recurrent pneumonia in the lesion
Paradoxical embolic stroke
Stridor from compression of the trachea
Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy
approach: Identify the lesion: lung tissue with a systemic arterial supply from the aorta and no bronchial connection is a pulmonary sequestration.
Separate it from a bronchogenic cyst, which is usually mediastinal, fluid filled, and has no aortic feeding vessel.
Predict the problem: tissue that cannot clear secretions through a bronchus becomes infected again and again.
questions.why: Pulmonary sequestration is a mass of nonfunctioning lung tissue that develops from an accessory foregut bud. It has no normal connection to the airways and gets its blood from a systemic artery, usually from the aorta. Intralobar sequestration, which lies within a lower lobe, often becomes infected through small pores, and secretions cannot drain, so recurrent pneumonia in the same spot is typical. Bronchogenic cysts also come from abnormal foregut budding but are usually fluid-filled cysts in the mediastinum that may compress the airway.
whyNot: Correct.

Paradoxical embolism needs a right-to-left shunt, such as a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation. A sequestration is fed by systemic arterial blood and does not shunt venous blood to the systemic side.
Tracheal compression with stridor fits a mediastinal bronchogenic cyst near the carina, not a lesion in the lower lobe.
Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy is mainly a paraneoplastic finding with lung cancer, especially adenocarcinoma.

questions.stem: While awaiting surgery, he cries forcefully and gastric contents reflux through the distal fistula into his trachea. Within 2 hours, he becomes tachypneic and hypoxemic, and a chest radiograph shows new infiltrates in the right upper and both lower lung zones. Which of the following best explains this early lung injury?
options: Infection with aspirated oral anaerobic bacteria
Chemical injury from acidic gastric contents
Hospital-acquired MRSA pneumonia
Transient tachypnea from retained fetal lung fluid
approach: Note the timing: lung injury within hours of aspirating gastric contents.
Separate chemical pneumonitis, which begins within hours from acid injury, from bacterial aspiration pneumonia, which develops over days.
Use the setting: hospital-acquired infections such as MRSA need about 48 hours or more in hospital.
questions.why: Gastric acid that reaches the airways injures the alveolar epithelium and capillaries within minutes to hours. This chemical pneumonitis causes rapid hypoxemia and infiltrates in dependent lung segments, before bacteria have time to multiply. Bacterial aspiration pneumonia, from oral anaerobes and streptococci, develops over days and can form an abscess. Hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia, after 48 hours or more, are usually caused by Pseudomonas, MRSA, and enteric gram-negative rods.
whyNot: Bacterial aspiration pneumonia from oral anaerobes develops over days. A newborn also has little oral anaerobic flora.
Correct.
Hospital-acquired pneumonia is defined as starting 48 hours or more after admission. Bacterial infection would not cause infiltrates within 2 hours.
Transient tachypnea of the newborn starts at birth and clears in 1 to 2 days. It does not appear suddenly after a reflux event.

dx: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia with pulmonary hypoplasia
case: A female newborn delivered at 39 weeks' gestation has severe respiratory distress and cyanosis within minutes of birth. Temperature is 36.6 °C (97.9 °F), pulse is 170/min, respirations are 72/min, and blood pressure is 52/30 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 92% in the right hand and 75% in the right foot on 100% oxygen. The abdomen is sunken. Breath sounds are absent over the left chest, and heart sounds are loudest to the right of the sternum. A chest radiograph shows gas-filled bowel loops in the left hemithorax, a small left lung, and shift of the mediastinum to the right. Echocardiography shows right-to-left shunting across the ductus arteriosus. Diagnosis: congenital diaphragmatic hernia with pulmonary hypoplasia.

questions.stem: Her defect is in the posterolateral part of the left hemidiaphragm. Which of the following developmental errors most likely caused it?
options: Defect between the sternal and costal origins of the diaphragm
Failed closure of the left pleuroperitoneal membrane
Failed muscularization of an intact diaphragmatic dome
Widening of the esophageal hiatus around the stomach
approach: Recall the parts that form the diaphragm: septum transversum, pleuroperitoneal membranes, dorsal mesentery of the esophagus, and body wall muscle.
Match the posterolateral location to the pleuroperitoneal membranes, which close the pleuroperitoneal canals.
Note why the left side is affected most: the left canal closes later than the right.
questions.why: Most congenital diaphragmatic hernias are posterolateral (Bochdalek) defects, about 85% on the left. They occur when a pleuroperitoneal membrane fails to close its pleuroperitoneal canal. Abdominal organs move into the chest while the lungs are growing, compress the lung on that side, and push the mediastinum away. The abdomen looks sunken (scaphoid) because the bowel is in the chest.
whyNot: A defect between the sternal and costal origins is an anterior (Morgagni) hernia. It is less common and usually on the right.
Correct.
Failed muscularization leaves a thin but intact membrane, which is eventration of the diaphragm. Bowel stays below the membrane.
Widening of the esophageal hiatus is a hiatal hernia, an acquired condition usually seen in adults.

questions.stem: In the same nursery, a newborn boy with bilateral renal agenesis has a similar degree of respiratory failure from small lungs. Which of the following is the shared mechanism of lung injury in these two infants?
options: Deficient surfactant from immature type II pneumocytes
Aspiration of meconium-stained fluid during delivery
Infection of the amniotic fluid before birth
Restricted lung expansion during fetal development
approach: Explain the boy's lungs: no kidneys means no fetal urine, so oligohydramnios develops and the uterus compresses the chest.
Explain the girl's lungs: abdominal organs in the chest take up the space the lung needs.
Find the common factor: the fetal lungs cannot expand with fetal breathing and lung fluid, so too few airways and alveoli form, which leads to respiratory failure at birth.
questions.why: Fetal lungs need room to grow and need to be stretched by lung fluid and fetal breathing movements. In bilateral renal agenesis, no urine means oligohydramnios, so the chest is compressed and lung fluid is lost (the Potter sequence). In diaphragmatic hernia, bowel in the chest compresses the lung. Both cause pulmonary hypoplasia with fewer airway branches, alveoli, and vessels, so the newborn cannot exchange gas well even with normal surfactant.
whyNot: Surfactant deficiency causes respiratory distress in preterm infants. Both of these infants have lungs that are too small, which is a different problem.
Meconium aspiration occurs around birth in post-term or stressed infants and does not explain small lungs.
Chorioamnionitis can cause neonatal pneumonia and sepsis, but it does not explain underdeveloped lungs in both infants.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her hypoplastic left lung stays at a very low volume despite ventilation. Apart from any effect of low oxygen, which of the following best explains the high vascular resistance in that lung at this volume?
options: Compression of alveolar capillaries by distended alveoli
Recruitment and distension of previously closed capillaries
Extra-alveolar vessel narrowing from lost radial traction
Greater radial traction pulling open the larger vessels
approach: Recall that pulmonary vascular resistance is lowest near functional residual capacity.
Separate the two vessel types: extra-alveolar vessels are held open by the pull of surrounding tissue, and alveolar capillaries are squeezed by expanding alveoli.
Apply to low volume: the tissue pull is lost, extra-alveolar vessels narrow, and resistance rises.
questions.why: Pulmonary vascular resistance follows a U-shaped curve with lung volume, lowest near FRC. At low lung volumes, the lung tissue does not pull outward on the larger extra-alveolar vessels, so they narrow and resistance rises. At high lung volumes, the stretched alveoli compress the capillaries in their walls, which also raises resistance. Her small, poorly inflated lung sits on the low-volume side of this curve.
whyNot: Compression of alveolar capillaries by stretched alveoli raises resistance at high lung volumes, not at low ones.
Recruitment and distension of capillaries lower resistance, as happens when pulmonary blood flow rises during exercise.
Correct.
Radial traction increases as the lung inflates. At low volume it is reduced, so this choice describes the wrong direction.

topics: Pulmonary vascular resistance and lung volume

questions.stem: Her oxygen saturation is higher in the right hand than in the foot because her pulmonary artery pressure exceeds aortic pressure. In addition to her small vascular bed, which of the following mechanisms in her lungs most likely raises the pulmonary arterial pressure?
options: Hypoxic constriction of pulmonary arteriolar smooth muscle
Hypoxia-induced dilation of pulmonary arterioles via KATP channels
Excess endothelial nitric oxide release in the pulmonary bed
Increased prostacyclin synthesis by pulmonary endothelium
approach: Read the saturation gap: blood in the foot gets deoxygenated blood shunted right to left through the ductus, so pulmonary pressure is high.
Recall how pulmonary vessels respond to low alveolar oxygen: they constrict, the opposite of systemic arterioles.
Link poorly ventilated, hypoxic lung to widespread vasoconstriction and persistent pulmonary hypertension.
questions.why: In the lung, low alveolar oxygen constricts the small pulmonary arteries. This normally shifts blood away from poorly ventilated areas. When much of the lung is hypoxic, the constriction is widespread and raises pulmonary artery pressure. In this newborn, the high pressure keeps fetal pathways open, so deoxygenated blood crosses the ductus arteriosus into the descending aorta and the foot saturation is lower than the hand. Over time, chronic alveolar hypoxia from lung disease causes pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular hypertrophy (cor pulmonale). Systemic arterioles do the opposite and dilate with hypoxia.
whyNot: Correct.
Hypoxic dilation through KATP channels is the response of systemic arterioles, such as coronary and skeletal muscle vessels, not pulmonary ones.
Nitric oxide relaxes pulmonary vessels. That is why inhaled nitric oxide is used to lower pulmonary pressure in newborns.
Prostacyclin is a pulmonary vasodilator. More of it would lower pulmonary pressure.

topics: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

case: A 19-year-old woman in basic military training comes to the clinic because of a 10-day history of headache, sore throat, malaise, and a persistent dry cough. Several recruits in her barracks have had similar symptoms. Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg. She does not appear acutely ill. A few scattered crackles are heard at both lung bases. A chest radiograph shows patchy bilateral interstitial infiltrates that are more extensive than the physical findings suggest. Arterial blood gas analysis at sea level on room air shows pH 7.46 (7.35 to 7.45), PaCO2 32 mm Hg (35 to 45), and PaO2 64 mm Hg (75 to 100). Sputum Gram stain shows a few neutrophils and no organisms. PCR of a throat swab detects Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Diagnosis: Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia.

questions.stem: Two weeks later, she has fatigue, pallor, and dark urine, and her fingertips turn blue after outdoor drills in cold weather. Hemoglobin concentration is 9.6 g/dL (12 to 16), and the direct antiglobulin test is positive for C3 only. Which of the following best explains her anemia?
options: Warm-reactive IgG against erythrocyte Rh antigens
Complement lysis from loss of CD55 and CD59 anchors
Cold-reactive IgM to I antigen fixing complement
Shearing of erythrocytes by microthrombi in arterioles
approach: Link the clues: hemolysis with symptoms in the cold and a direct antiglobulin test positive for complement only.
Recall the antibody that Mycoplasma pneumoniae induces: cold agglutinins, which are IgM against the I antigen on red cells.
Explain the C3 result: IgM binds in the cool periphery, fixes complement, and then falls off as blood warms, leaving C3 on the cell.
questions.why: Mycoplasma pneumoniae often stimulates IgM antibodies that cross-react with the I antigen on red cells. These cold agglutinins bind in cool fingers and toes, fix complement, and then detach in the warm core, so the antiglobulin test shows C3 but no IgG. Complement causes hemolysis, mostly through liver macrophages, and sometimes directly in vessels. Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall, so it does not appear on Gram stain and is not killed by beta-lactam antibiotics. Its pneumonia is typically mild in young adults living in close quarters, and the radiograph looks worse than the patient.
whyNot: Warm IgG autoantibodies cause warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, with a direct antiglobulin test positive for IgG. Symptoms do not depend on cold.
Loss of CD55 and CD59 is paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. The direct antiglobulin test is negative.
Correct.
Microangiopathic hemolysis shows schistocytes and a negative direct antiglobulin test, as in TTP or hemolytic uremic syndrome.

questions.stem: She is given 40% oxygen by face mask, and her PaO2 rises to 150 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of her hypoxemia on room air?
options: Ventilation-perfusion mismatch
Right-to-left intrapulmonary shunt
Alveolar hypoventilation
Reduced inspired oxygen tension
approach: Rule out low inspired oxygen: she is at sea level on room air.
Rule out hypoventilation: her PaCO2 is low, so she is breathing more, not less.
Use the oxygen response: a large rise in PaO2 with supplemental oxygen fits ventilation-perfusion mismatch, while a true shunt barely responds.
questions.why: Patchy inflammation in pneumonia leaves some alveoli poorly ventilated but still perfused, which is ventilation-perfusion mismatch. These low V/Q units deliver poorly oxygenated blood, and the A-a gradient widens. Extra inspired oxygen raises the alveolar PO2 even in poorly ventilated units, so PaO2 rises sharply. In a true shunt, blood passes alveoli that receive no gas at all, so added oxygen cannot reach it and PaO2 barely changes. Hypoventilation and low inspired oxygen both keep the A-a gradient normal.
whyNot: Correct.
A right-to-left shunt sends blood past completely unventilated alveoli, so supplemental oxygen raises PaO2 very little.
Hypoventilation raises PaCO2. Her PaCO2 is low.
Low inspired oxygen occurs at high altitude or with a faulty gas supply. She is at sea level breathing room air.

questions.stem: A second recruit returns from 2 weeks of leave on her family's sheep farm, where she helped deliver lambs. She develops high fever, severe headache, dry cough, and patchy infiltrates with a normal mediastinal width on chest radiograph. Serum ALT concentration is 160 U/L (10 to 40). Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?
options: Francisella tularensis
Bacillus anthracis
Burkholderia pseudomallei
Coxiella burnetii
approach: Pick out the exposure: contact with birth products of sheep.
Match it to the organism that is concentrated in placentas and birth fluids of farm animals: Coxiella burnetii, the cause of Q fever.
Confirm with the picture: atypical pneumonia with hepatitis and a normal mediastinum.
questions.why: Coxiella burnetii causes Q fever. Infected sheep, goats, and cattle shed huge numbers of organisms in placentas and birth fluids, and people inhale contaminated dust or aerosols. Acute Q fever causes fever, headache, atypical pneumonia, and hepatitis. Coxiella forms a spore-like form that survives in the environment, and it does not need an arthropod vector to infect people.
whyNot: Francisella tularensis is acquired from rabbits, ticks, or deer flies and causes tularemia, usually with an ulcer and swollen lymph nodes.
Bacillus anthracis is acquired from spores in wool or hides. Inhalational anthrax causes hemorrhagic mediastinitis with a widened mediastinum, and her mediastinum is normal.
Burkholderia pseudomallei lives in soil and water in Southeast Asia and northern Australia and causes melioidosis.
Correct.

questions.stem: Using her room-air blood gas values at sea level (barometric pressure 760 mm Hg, water vapor pressure 47 mm Hg, respiratory quotient 0.8), which of the following is closest to her alveolar-arterial (A-a) oxygen gradient?
options: About 10 mm Hg
About 46 mm Hg
About 54 mm Hg
About 86 mm Hg
approach: Calculate PAO2: 0.21 times (760 minus 47) minus 32/0.8 = 149.7 minus 40 = about 110 mm Hg.
Subtract PaO2: 110 minus 64 = about 46 mm Hg.
Interpret: a normal gradient for a young adult is about 5 to 15 mm Hg, so hers is widened, which points to a problem in the lung itself.
questions.why: The alveolar gas equation is PAO2 = FiO2 times (Patm minus 47) minus PaCO2/0.8. For her, 0.21 times 713 is about 150, and 32/0.8 is 40, so PAO2 is about 110 mm Hg. Subtracting her PaO2 of 64 gives an A-a gradient of about 46 mm Hg. A widened gradient means oxygen is not moving normally from alveoli into blood, as with V/Q mismatch, shunt, or diffusion limitation. Hypoventilation and high altitude lower PaO2 with a normal gradient.
whyNot: About 10 mm Hg is a normal gradient. Her low PaO2 together with a low PaCO2 cannot give a normal gradient.
Correct.
About 54 mm Hg comes from subtracting PaCO2 itself instead of PaCO2 divided by 0.8.
About 86 mm Hg comes from leaving out the PaCO2 term entirely.
